_meta.section: Living as Christians Part 7 — Discussion: 'Follow the Course of Hospitality'
_meta.discussion_questions: data-pids 32 (video Q), 34 (benefit-from-showing), 37 (learn from Jehovah's example), 39 (extend outside circle), 41 (Bible examples)
_meta.preparation_standard: v12 LAC — all 4 discussion comments redrafted to the different-domain standard. Both versions stored per note: primary `content` ships to JW Library; `alternate_content` is the prior version preserved for Tyler's day-of call. ¶32: workplace grief / Mary-Martha. ¶37: streetlights / Acts 14:17 + Mt 5:45. ¶39: elevator / Mt 25 sheep. ¶41: Marcus took the blame at work / Rahab in Joshua 2 + Heb 11:31 + Mt 1:5 (Jesus' genealogy).

notes.content: When my coworker's husband died last spring, somebody from the building came and sat with her in her office for two hours. Didn't bring food. Didn't say much. Just sat with her. That's what she still talks about. Now look at Luke 10. Martha had Jesus in her house — Jesus — and she was so distracted with the meal she got mad at her sister Mary, who was just sitting at his feet. 'Tell her to help me,' she said. And Jesus answered: 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious about many things. Mary has chosen the good portion.' Notice — Jesus didn't say the meal didn't matter. He said anxiety about the meal had a cost. The cost was Mary's seat next to him. Most of us think hospitality is what we DO for somebody. Mary chose to do nothing for him, and Jesus called it 'the good portion.' So when somebody walks into our home or our office or our hospital room, the question isn't what we prepared. It's whether we can put it down and just sit with them. Hospitality at its best isn't a meal. It's a chair pulled up beside you.
notes.alternate_content: There's two kinds of hostess in your life. There's the one who's stressed in the kitchen, asks 'are you hungry?' three times, and won't sit down. And there's the one who hears the doorbell, puts down the spoon, and sits with you while the food cooks itself. My grandma was the second kind. Look at Luke 10. Martha had Jesus in her house — Jesus — and she was so distracted with the meal she got mad that her sister Mary was just sitting at his feet. 'Tell her to help me,' she said. And Jesus answered: 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious about many things. Mary has chosen the good portion.' Notice — Jesus didn't say the meal didn't matter. He said anxiety about the meal had a cost. The cost was Mary's seat next to him. Hospitality at its best isn't whether the food is hot. It's whether the host can put it down. So when somebody comes to our home or our table, the question isn't whether we prepared enough. It's whether we can stop preparing long enough to be with them. Martha was making dinner. Mary was making memory.

notes.content: The streetlights in my neighborhood come on around 7:30. They don't know who's walking under them. Could be the nurse heading to night shift. Could be the kid coming home from practice. Could be somebody who just got out of jail. Same light. Now look at Acts 14:17. Paul and Barnabas told the people of Lystra — most of whom didn't know Jehovah — that he 'gave you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling you to the full with food and good cheer.' The rain came down on people who didn't know his name. Then Jesus brings it forward in Matthew 5:45 — 'he makes his sun rise on both the wicked and the good and makes it rain on both the righteous and the unrighteous.' Notice what Jesus says next — that THIS is the proof of being his Father's child. Not that you love your friends. Anybody can do that. But that you keep the streetlight on for people who'd never thank you for it. So when we extend hospitality to people who can't pay us back, we're not being generous. We're being our Father's children. The plate isn't a gift. It's a family resemblance.
notes.alternate_content: My dad would feed any hungry person who showed up at our door. Didn't matter if they were a neighbor, a stranger, or somebody he'd never see again. Mom asked him once why he kept doing it. He said, 'Because somebody fed me when I was hungry.' Now look at Acts 14:17. Paul and Barnabas told the people of Lystra that Jehovah 'left witness of himself in doing good, giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling you to the full with food and good cheer.' Notice the audience. People who didn't know his name. Didn't acknowledge him. The rain came down anyway. Then Jesus brings it forward in Matthew 5:45 — 'he makes his sun rise on both the wicked and the good and makes it rain on both the righteous and the unrighteous.' That's the proof of sonship — your hospitality looks like the Father's. So when we extend our table to people who aren't part of our circle, who haven't earned it, who can't reciprocate — that's not us being generous. That's us being our Father's children. The plate isn't a gift. It's a family resemblance.

notes.content: I held the elevator for a guy at my building once. Standard thing. He stepped in and his eyes were red. He looked at me and said, 'thank you, man, I'm on my way to my dad's hospital room and I'm really late.' Twenty seconds. Doors closed. Never saw him again. Now look at Matthew 25. Jesus is describing the day of judgment, and he separates people based on one thing — did they feed the hungry, take in the stranger, visit the sick. The sheep are confused. They say, 'Lord, when did we see YOU hungry? When did we see YOU thirsty?' They don't know they were doing it for him. And Jesus answers: 'whatever you did to one of the least of these brothers of mine, you did to me.' Notice — the sheep are surprised. The kindness was offered without weight. So when we hold a door, hold an elevator, give somebody our seat on the train — the question isn't whether they deserve it. It's whether we know what we're actually holding open. The kindness we think is small might be sitting at a hospital bed.
notes.alternate_content: There's a guy who sleeps at the gas station near my apartment. I started bringing him a sandwich about a year ago. Nothing dramatic — just a sandwich. And one Saturday he wasn't there, and I realized I didn't actually know his name. Then look at Matthew 25. Jesus is describing the day of judgment, and he separates people based on one thing — did they feed the hungry, take in the stranger, visit the sick. The sheep are confused. They say, 'Lord, when did we see YOU hungry?' They don't know they were doing it for him. And Jesus answers: 'whatever you did to one of the least of these brothers of mine, you did to me.' That's the move. Hospitality to people outside our circle isn't us being generous. It's us hosting Jesus without knowing it. So when we extend our table to somebody who can't pay us back, who we'd normally walk past, the question isn't whether they deserved it. The question is who else might be sitting at our table. The sandwich isn't for the man at the gas station. It's for whoever Jesus says he is.

notes.content: There was a guy at my old job named Marcus. I was on probation. I made a mistake on a delivery one Tuesday, expensive one. Marcus walked into the manager's office before I could say anything and took the blame. Got a write-up for something he didn't do. He had no skin in my career. He just had the seat next to mine. Now look at Joshua 2. Rahab — a Gentile prostitute in Jericho — hides two Israelite spies on her roof. Hiding foreign spies wasn't hospitality. It was a death sentence if she got caught. She'd known these men for what, an afternoon? She bet her life on them. Hebrews 11:31 says 'by faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish, because she received the spies in a peaceful way.' And Matthew 1:5 — that same Rahab is in Jesus' genealogy. Ancestor of the Messiah. That afternoon hospitality ran her name into the Bible's most important family tree. So when we extend hospitality to somebody who can't pay us back, the question isn't what we lose. It's what we don't yet know we're stepping into.
notes.alternate_content: Other Bible examples of hospitality worth remembering — Abraham running to meet the three strangers in Genesis 18, slaughtering the calf, standing to serve them. Lot insisting the angels stay with him in Genesis 19. Rahab hiding the spies on her roof in Joshua 2. The widow of Zarephath sharing her last meal with Elijah in 1 Kings 17. Notice the pattern across all of them — none of these people knew the long-term outcome of their hospitality. They just opened the door. Abraham didn't know Sarah would conceive. The widow didn't know her flour wouldn't run out. Hospitality isn't transactional. It's offered first, blessed after.

underlines.phrase: consider how you would like to show hospitality
